claims.text: A conventional automotive exhaust catalyst consists of platinum dispersed on an alumina support.
Approximately 5 wt% cerium should be incorporated into the alumina support before platinum deposition.
Typical automotive exhaust operation includes temperatures from 300°C to 800°C, redox cycling, and thermal aging.
Cerium incorporation forms cerium oxide clusters within the alumina matrix.
Cerium oxide clusters in alumina increase the density of oxygen vacancies.
Enhanced metal-support interactions improve platinum dispersion.
Cerium incorporation enhances the oxygen-storage capacity of the support.
The increased oxygen-vacancy density improves oxygen mobility at the catalyst surface.
Improved oxygen mobility and cerium modification stabilize platinum nanoparticles against sintering.
Suppression of platinum sintering maintains high platinum dispersion after thermal aging.
The cerium-doped catalyst will have higher CO conversion efficiency than standard Pt on undoped alumina.
The cerium-doped catalyst will have higher hydrocarbon conversion efficiency than standard Pt on undoped alumina.
The cerium-doped catalyst will have higher NOx conversion efficiency than standard Pt on undoped alumina.
The cerium-doped catalyst will retain more catalytic activity after thermal aging than standard Pt on undoped alumina.
Cerium modification will permit reduced platinum loading while maintaining or improving catalytic activity.
The expected benefits may change outside 300–800°C or standard redox-cycling conditions.
Significant changes from approximately 5 wt% cerium may alter the expected benefits.
Prior evidence supports cerium-induced enhancement of oxygen-storage capacity and metal-support interactions.

contradictions.description: The conditions state that no other system parameters will change, but the proposed test changes both cerium content and platinum loading relative to the baseline. This also confounds the effect of cerium incorporation with the effect of reduced platinum loading.
